q: Which process aggregates the cost estimates of activities or work packages into an authorized cost baseline?
explanation: Develop Budget aggregates the estimated costs to establish an authorized cost baseline, against which performance is monitored and controlled.

q: What are the main outputs of the Plan Financial Management process?
options: Financial management plan and funding strategy
Cost baseline and the project funding requirements
Cost estimates and the basis of estimates
explanation: Plan Financial Management produces the financial management plan and the funding strategy. The cost baseline comes from Develop Budget, cost estimates from Estimate Costs, and forecasts from Monitor and Control Finances.

q: According to the PMBOK Guide, where does the value of financial measurement lie?
options: In collecting as much cost data as possible
In sending reports to every stakeholder weekly
In proving that the estimate was correct
In the decisions and actions the data leads to
explanation: The value is not in collecting and spreading the data, but in the interactions about how to use it to make value-adding, well-informed decisions and take action.

q: A project buys new servers that will be owned by the organization for years. Which type of expenditure is this usually?
explanation: CapEx are funds invested to acquire, upgrade and maintain physical assets such as buildings, technology or equipment. OpEx covers the ongoing costs of running the business, such as wages, rent and utilities.

q: The department's project money must be spent within the fiscal year and cannot move to the next year. What is this an example of?
explanation: Budget is the main financial constraint, but not the only one: money may be tied to a type (CapEx or OpEx), a purpose, or a period such as a fiscal year.

q: Funds are released to the project one phase at a time, after each phase gate. Which funding strategy is this?
explanation: In incremental disbursement, funds are secured and allocated in several increments, tied to phases or key milestones. A lump sum allocates the whole budget and reserves at once.

q: The sponsor needs a cost figure by tomorrow to decide whether to fund the next phase. The WBS is not built yet, but a similar project closed last year. Which technique fits, and what is its trade-off?
explanation: Analogous estimating uses values from a similar past project. It is less costly and time-consuming than other techniques but can be less accurate, and fits when detailed information is limited. Bottom-up needs the WBS.
options: Bottom-up: the most accurate, but it takes days
Parametric: needs no historical data at all
Analogous: quick and cheap, but less accurate

q: A builder estimates a 500 square meter building at 1,200 per square meter, based on data from many past buildings. Which technique is this?
explanation: Parametric estimating uses a statistical relationship between historical data and a parameter, such as square footage in construction, to calculate the estimate.

q: A work package's cost estimates are 40,000 optimistic, 55,000 most likely and 85,000 pessimistic. What is the triangular three-point estimate?
explanation: Triangular distribution: (40,000 + 55,000 + 85,000) / 3 = 180,000 / 3 = 60,000. The beta (PERT) formula, (O + 4M + P) / 6, would give 57,500.

q: At project start, the team gives a rough order of magnitude estimate. Which accuracy range is typical for it?
explanation: A ROM estimate in the start-up phase may be in the range of −25% to +75%. Later, with more information, estimates narrow, for example to −10%/+15%. (The Sixth Edition's definitive estimate is −5% to +10%.)

q: Why does the accuracy of project cost estimates usually improve as the project goes on?
options: Because the sponsor approves larger reserves later
Because the team works faster near the end
Because the cost baseline is reset every month
Because more is known and assumptions get tested
explanation: Cost estimates are reviewed and refined as more detail becomes available and assumptions are tested, so accuracy increases through the life cycle.

q: Rework on some deliverables is expected, but its amount is not known. How should the team budget for it?
options: As management reserve outside the baseline
As contingency reserve within the cost baseline
As hidden padding added to every activity estimate
By leaving it out until the rework happens
explanation: Anticipated rework of unknown size is a known-unknown. Contingency reserves cover identified risks, are clearly identified in the cost documents, and are part of the cost baseline.

q: Halfway through, the project manager checks whether the remaining contingency is enough for the remaining risks. Which technique is this?
explanation: Reserve analysis evaluates the amount of risk and the schedule and budget reserve, to decide whether the reserve is sufficient for the remaining risk.

q: An identified risk occurs, and the team uses 15,000 of the 60,000 contingency reserve, as its planned response says. What happens to the cost baseline?
explanation: Contingency reserves are part of the cost baseline, allocated for identified risks. Using them as planned does not change the baseline. Only management reserve, which sits outside the baseline, needs an approved change when used.
options: It stays the same: the contingency is already in it
It rises by 15,000 through an approved change
It falls by 15,000, as the reserve is spent
It is rebuilt from new bottom-up estimates

q: The project budget is 1,000,000. It includes a management reserve of 80,000 and a contingency reserve of 70,000. What is the cost baseline?
explanation: Cost baseline = project budget − management reserve = 1,000,000 − 80,000 = 920,000. It still contains the 70,000 contingency; the work estimates alone are 850,000.

q: Unforeseen work within scope appears, and senior management releases part of the management reserve. What must happen to the cost baseline?
options: Nothing at all, since the reserve sits outside the baseline
The amount is added through an approved change
The baseline is rebuilt from new estimates
The contingency reserve is reduced to match
explanation: Management reserve is not in the cost baseline. When some of it funds unforeseen work, that amount is added to the cost baseline, which requires an approved change.

q: Planned spending in the third quarter exceeds the funding limit for that quarter. What should the project manager do?
options: Ask the team to stop all work until the next quarter
Move the excess into the management reserve
Reschedule work to level the rate of spending
Raise the funding limit in the financial plan
explanation: Funding limit reconciliation compares planned spending with funding limits. A variance may require rescheduling work to level the rate of expenditure, using imposed date constraints.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Funding limit reconciliation

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Funding limit reconciliation

q: From which document are the total and periodic project funding requirements derived?
explanation: Project funding requirements, total and periodic, are derived from the cost baseline. Total funds are the cost baseline plus management reserve.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Project funding requirements

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Project funding requirements

q: Which part of the financial management plan says how much cost variance is allowed before action must be taken?
explanation: Control thresholds set the agreed variation allowed before action, usually as a percentage deviation from the baseline plan.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Financial management plan

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Financial management plan

q: Which WBS component is used for project cost accounting and carries a code that links to the organization's accounting system?
explanation: The WBS component used for project cost accounting is the control account. Each one has a unique code or account number linked to the accounting system.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Financial management plan

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 4, Financial management plan

q: Cost performance has moved past the agreed control threshold. What should the project manager do?
options: Use the management reserve quietly to cover it
Wait to see whether the trend corrects itself
Analyze the cause and raise a change request
Lower the threshold so that no action is needed
explanation: Monitor and Control Finances uses variance analysis to find deviations and their causes, then takes corrective action; changes to the cost baseline go through change control as change requests.

q: How does the PMBOK Guide say an iterative approach affects project spending?
options: It flattens the spent curve over the project
It moves most spending to the final release
It removes the need for any financial control
It requires one lump sum paid at the start
explanation: Iterative approaches flatten the spent curve. Financial planning and controls are tailored, using time-phased budgeting and continuous funding assessment.

q: In a project using an agile approach, how may the budget be allocated, according to the PMBOK Guide?
options: Once, as a lump sum fixed for the entire project
Only after the final increment is accepted
By the sponsor approving each user story's cost
For a quarter, then revised by the work achieved
explanation: In agile projects, the budget can be allocated for a quarter and then revised quarterly, which gives more flexibility based on the amount of work achieved.

q: A small project has very limited financial flexibility. Which approach to reserves does the PMBOK Guide suggest?
options: No reserves, to keep the budget as low as possible
Conservative budgeting with both kinds of reserve
Only management reserve, held by the sponsor
Reserves set only after the first cost overrun
explanation: For a small project with limited financial flexibility, a conservative approach to budgeting with contingency and management reserves helps mitigate risks and keep the project stable.

q: A key machine is scarce this year and rental surcharges are expected. The project manager raises the cost forecast now. Which finance enabler is this?
options: Managing claims under the procurement contract
explanation: Resource constraints can raise actual and forecast costs through surcharges, rush shipping or penalties. Spotting this early is anticipating future finance challenges.

q: Which THREE are tools and techniques of the Estimate Costs process?
explanation: Figure 2-28 lists expert judgment, analogous, parametric, bottom-up and multipoint estimating, alternatives and reserve analysis, cost of quality, the PMIS and voting. Cost aggregation, funding limit reconciliation and financing belong to Develop Budget.

q: Which TWO are tools and techniques of the Develop Budget process?
explanation: Figure 2-29 lists expert judgment, cost aggregation, reserve analysis, historical information review, funding limit reconciliation and financing. Analogous and multipoint estimating belong to Estimate Costs.

q: Which TWO are financial constraints other than the total budget?
explanation: Budget is the main financial constraint but not the only one. The project may be restricted to a type of money (CapEx or OpEx, internal or external personnel) or to funds for a specific purpose or period, such as a fiscal year.
options: Money that may be spent only as CapEx or OpEx
Funds that must be used within the fiscal year
The number of people on the team

q: Match each estimating technique with how it works.
right: Uses actual values from a similar past project
Applies an algorithm to historical data and parameters
Aggregates estimates of the lowest-level work
Averages optimistic, most likely and pessimistic values
explanation: Analogous is quick but less accurate; bottom-up is the most detailed; parametric is as good as its data; multipoint shows the range of uncertainty.

q: Complete each statement about reserves and the budget.

blanks.text: Identified risks with planned responses are covered by the
The cost baseline plus the management reserve equals the
Unforeseen work within scope is covered by the

explanation: Contingency reserve is inside the cost baseline for known risks; management reserve is outside it for unknown-unknowns; together with the baseline it makes the project budget.
